definition: Contemporaneous means existing or occurring during the same period of time.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word contemporaneous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know contemporaneous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The two grandmothers were contemporaneous, born the same spring on opposite sides of the world, though their paths never crossed.
Overlapping claims only that two spans share some stretch; contemporaneous sets both things inside the same period outright.
Synchronized goes past contemporaneous — not merely sharing an era, but matched beat for beat to the very same instant.

Coexisting things share the world at the same time and usually stand side by side — two species in one pond, rival shops on one street. Contemporaneous is the cooler, historian's word: it says only that two things belong to the same period, whether or not they ever meet.

Concurrent means running at the same moment — two meetings held at once, prison sentences served side by side. It is tighter than contemporaneous, which asks only that two things share the same period, even a loose stretch of years.

Pub-quiz history runs on the shock of the contemporaneous: the last woolly mammoths were still grazing an Arctic island while the pyramids were rising in Egypt, and Oxford dons were lecturing two hundred years before the Aztec capital was founded.
Nothing connects these pairs except the calendar — which is precisely the surprise.
Contemporaneous is the exact word because it names things existing or occurring during the same period of time — the same slice of the calendar, whether or not they ever touched.
It makes no claim of connection, influence, or cause: two contemporaneous events may be tightly linked or utterly unrelated.
The word just sets two clocks side by side and notes that they agree.
Contemporaneous is the historian's and lawyer's word for things that share the same period.

This unit's coincidental answers a different question — not when two things happened, but whether chance explains their pairing: contemporaneous events may be deeply linked; coincidental ones are not.
For things striking at the very same instant, plainer phrases like 'at once' do the job.

For its centennial, the museum hung two landscape paintings side by side: one from Kyoto, one from a village in Norway.
The painters were contemporaneous — both worked in the 1870s — though neither ever saw the other's country, spoke the other's language, or knew the other existed.
Visitors kept asking which artist had influenced which.
The curator's wall text answered before they could: no letters, no exhibitions in common, no shared teacher.
What the pairing showed was subtler — two people, an ocean apart, answering the same decade's light with the same restless brushwork.
The show's title made the argument in two words: 'Same Hour.'
